title: Remote Repositories
tagline: GitHub doesn't do anything Git itself can't -- it's just a server hosting a copy of your repo.

concept.label: What
concept.text: A remote is a named reference to a copy of your repo elsewhere -- origin is the default name for "where I cloned/pushed this from".

concept.label: Why
concept.text: Local commits only exist on your machine until you push them -- a remote is how work becomes shared and backed up.

concept.label: How
concept.text: git clone copies a remote repo locally; git push sends commits up; git pull brings new ones down.

concept.label: When
concept.text: Starting a new shared project (create on GitHub, clone it) or joining an existing one (clone someone else's).

concept.label: Where
concept.text: Every collaborative workflow from here on assumes a remote exists.

mnemonic.label: C.P.P.
mnemonic.text: Clone (copy down) -> Push (send up) -> Pull (bring down again) -- the remote round-trip

sandboxNote.text: you'll need a free GitHub account and a new empty repo created there to run these for real -- GitHub's own "Create repository" page shows you the exact remote URL to use below.

code:
git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/YOUR-REPO.git
cd YOUR-REPO

echo "# My Project" > README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Add README"

git push origin main            # PUSH: send this commit up to GitHub
# refresh the repo page on github.com -- your commit is there

# on a DIFFERENT machine (or after someone else pushes):
git pull origin main            # PULL: fetch + merge their new commits in

cycle.title: Read the concept table once
cycle.text: The idea to hold onto: your local repo and GitHub's copy are just two independent Git repos that happen to know about each other by URL. Nothing GitHub does is Git-magic -- it's the same commands you already know, pointed at a server.

cycle.title: Type the code yourself — no copy-paste
cycle.text: Create a real (even empty) repo on github.com, clone it, and push a real commit. Refresh the GitHub page and actually watch your commit appear.
cycle.hint: If push is rejected, it almost always means the remote has commits you don't have locally yet -- that's Module 3's git pull, not a bug.

cycle.title: Apply it to your own data
cycle.text: Make three commits locally without pushing after each one, THEN push all three at once, and look at GitHub's commit history page to confirm all three show up individually, in order.

cycle.title: Reflect & note
cycle.text: What happened the first time push was rejected (if it was)? What did the error message actually say, and what fixed it?
cycle.placeholder: e.g. Got 'Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not have locally' -- I'd forgotten I'd edited the README directly on github.com earlier, so a git pull first resolved it...

cycle.title: Tick off before moving on
checklist: I can explain what a remote actually is (a URL, not magic).
I cloned a real repo from GitHub myself.
I pushed a real commit and watched it appear on github.com.
I made multiple local commits and pushed them together.
I wrote a reflection note above.
